title: Diagnose the cognitive biases in Marcus's hiring recommendation
object_of_analysis: Marcus (Senior Engineering Manager) is interviewing two candidates for a Senior Data Analyst role. Candidate A graduated from the same university as Marcus, presented with polished confidence, and scored at the 74th percentile on the technical assessment. Candidate B has an unconventional background, was visibly nervous during the interview, but scored at the 96th percentile on the technical assessment and submitted the strongest work sample of any candidate in the hiring round. After the interviews, Marcus recommends Candidate A, saying: 'Candidate B is technically strong but I'm not confident they have the leadership presence this role needs. Candidate A has the full package — technical competence plus the ability to command a room. That matters for a senior role.'
context: You are a People & Culture partner reviewing Marcus's hiring recommendation before it is finalised. You suspect the recommendation may be influenced by cognitive biases rather than job-relevant criteria. Using dual-process theory, identify the System 1 heuristics and biases that appear to have influenced Marcus's recommendation, explain the mechanism of each, and design a set of System 2 debiasing protocols that the organisation could implement to improve hiring decision quality.
instructions: Part 1: Identify at least four specific cognitive biases visible in Marcus's decision-making, using dual-process theory as your framework. For each bias, name it precisely, quote the evidence from the vignette that suggests it is operating, and explain the System 1 mechanism at work. Part 2: For each bias you identified, design a specific System 2 override protocol — a concrete procedural change that would force deliberate, criteria-based evaluation at the point where the bias is most likely to activate. Part 3: Reflect briefly on why Marcus's justification ('leadership presence', 'full package') feels compelling to him, even if it is biased — what does this tell us about the phenomenology of System 1 reasoning?

workspace_prompts.bias_identification: Read Marcus's recommendation carefully. What information is Marcus weighting heavily? What information is he underweighting? Who went to his university? What might 'leadership presence' and 'command a room' really be tracking? Look for: (1) a similarity-based preference, (2) an effect where one strong trait inflates assessment of other traits, (3) a double standard in how nervousness is interpreted for each candidate, (4) a tendency to discount objective predictive data in favour of subjective impressions.
workspace_prompts.system1_mechanisms: For each bias you find: describe the automatic, low-effort System 1 process that produced it. What pattern-matching or affect heuristic is at work? System 1 processes are: fast, automatic, associative, emotion-influenced, difficult to introspect. Marcus almost certainly believes his assessment is genuinely objective — this is a feature of System 1, not evidence of bad faith.
workspace_prompts.debiasing_protocols: Effective debiasing protocols work by inserting a System 2 check at the moment the bias is most likely to influence the decision. Think about: structured criteria weighted before interviews; blind evaluation stages; decision pre-commitment; structured interviews with the same questions in the same order; consider-the-opposite exercises. Design protocols specifically targeted at the biases you identified.
workspace_prompts.phenomenology: Marcus's recommendation feels right to him. He has constructed a post-hoc justification ('leadership presence') that makes the recommendation feel evidence-based. What does dual-process theory predict about this? How does the research on 'confabulation' (constructing explanations for decisions that were made on other grounds) apply here?

hints.title: Four biases to look for
hints.content: The four most clearly operating biases are: (1) Affinity bias (similarity-attraction effect) — Marcus and Candidate A share a university; research consistently shows people rate similar others more favourably on subjective dimensions; (2) Halo effect — Candidate A's polished presentation inflates Marcus's assessment of their overall capability; (3) Attribution asymmetry — the same behaviour (interview nervousness) is interpreted very differently for the two candidates; (4) Anchoring to less-predictive evidence — interview performance is given more weight than technical test scores and work samples, even though research on hiring predictive validity shows structured tests and work samples outpredict interview performance.

hints.title: Predictive validity research — what actually predicts job performance?
hints.content: The Schmidt & Hunter meta-analysis (1998, updated 2016) on the predictive validity of different selection methods found: general mental ability tests (r ≈ 0.51), work sample tests (r ≈ 0.54), structured interviews (r ≈ 0.51), unstructured interviews (r ≈ 0.38), and years of experience (r ≈ 0.18). The work sample test and technical assessment are among the most predictive instruments available. Marcus is anchoring on the least predictive instrument (unstructured interview impression) to override the most predictive instruments.

hints.title: The confabulation point for Part 3
hints.content: Research on the split-brain patients and subsequent broader cognitive psychology (Gazzaniga, Nisbett & Wilson 1977) establishes that humans routinely construct post-hoc verbal justifications for decisions that were driven by pre-conscious processes. The Left Hemisphere Interpreter (Gazzaniga) generates explanations that feel genuine and coherent but may not reflect the actual causal process. 'Leadership presence' is likely a confabulated justification — a label Marcus's verbal reasoning system produced to make sense of an affective preference that was actually produced by affinity bias and halo effect.

key_moves: BIAS 1 — AFFINITY BIAS (SIMILARITY-ATTRACTION EFFECT): Marcus and Candidate A share a university. Research (Byrne, 1997; Rivera, 2012) shows that similarity on dimensions like educational institution, background, and interests significantly inflates subjective assessments, even when evaluators believe they are assessing job-relevant criteria. The System 1 mechanism: automatic positive affect toward familiar/similar others, instantiated as a sense that the person 'fits' or 'has what we're looking for.'

BIAS 2 — HALO EFFECT: Candidate A's 'polished confidence' in the interview creates a positive general impression that inflates Marcus's assessment across all dimensions. 'Full package — technical competence plus ability to command a room' is the halo at work: one salient positive feature (confident presentation) inflates the overall evaluation. System 1 mechanism: global affect spreading — an emotional valence associated with one attribute transfers to assessment of unrelated attributes.

BIAS 3 — ATTRIBUTION ASYMMETRY (DOUBLE STANDARD): Candidate A's nervousness is not mentioned — either they weren't nervous, or nervousness in Candidate A was not treated as evidence of a character or competence deficit. Candidate B's nervousness is explicitly cited as evidence of lacking 'leadership presence.' The same behavioural signal (nervousness in an interview) is being interpreted very differently for the two candidates. System 1 mechanism: confirmation bias — when a candidate is already favoured (due to halo/affinity), their behaviours are interpreted charitably; when a candidate is already disfavoured, the same behaviours become evidence against them.

BIAS 4 — ANCHORING TO LOW-VALIDITY EVIDENCE: Marcus anchors his recommendation primarily on interview impression (lowest predictive validity selection instrument) while discounting the technical test (96th vs 74th percentile) and work sample (best of the cohort). This is not irrational in Marcus's subjective experience — the interview is vivid, emotionally salient, and feels like 'direct evidence.' The objective test scores are abstract numbers. System 1 weights vivid, recent, emotionally salient information more heavily than abstract statistical evidence (availability heuristic, affect heuristic).

DEBIASING PROTOCOLS: (1) Pre-interview criteria weighting: before any interview, team agrees on weighted criteria (technical skill: 40%, analytical problem-solving: 30%, communication: 20%, culture contribution: 10%); (2) Structured interview: same questions, same order, for all candidates; each answer scored against a rubric before moving to the next question; (3) Blind work sample evaluation: work samples evaluated without candidate identification before interviews occur; (4) Pre-commitment to evidence hierarchy: team agrees in advance that technical test and work sample scores will outweigh interview impression unless significant red flags emerge in structured interview; (5) Consider-the-opposite exercise: after making a recommendation, evaluator must write a paragraph arguing the opposite recommendation.
solution_sketch.revised_position: A System 2-informed recommendation for this role would: (1) weight the 96th percentile technical test and strongest work sample heavily (these are the most predictive instruments); (2) identify specifically what 'leadership presence' means in job-relevant, behavioural terms that can be tested; (3) note that interview nervousness in a capable candidate is not a reliable predictor of in-role communication performance; and (4) if 'command a room' communication style is genuinely job-critical, design a structured role-play or presentation exercise that tests it directly, rather than inferring it from an unstructured interview.
